JSON: Name: isogenic_pro_gbm_pipeline Title: An isogenic human stem-cell pipeline combining sequential CRISPR engineering, single-cell multi-omics, and perturbational genomics to map mutation-driven INSM1-dependent progenitor state transitions in glioblastoma Short Hypothesis: Sequential acquisition of TERT promoter C228T, TP53 loss-of-function, and PDGFRA D842V in human embryonic stem cell-derived neural stem cells causes a cell-state transition into an INSM1-driven neuronal intermediate progenitor-like program that is necessary for tumorigenicity; targeted inhibition of INSM1 will reduce the progenitor-like transcriptional program, metabolic reprogramming, and in vivo tumor formation. Related Work: Existing approaches to link canonical glioblastoma drivers to cell-state and epigenetic programs have relied on bulk profiling, genetically engineered mouse models, patient-derived xenografts, and primary glioma stem cell cultures. Bulk profiles identify subtype signatures but cannot resolve intratumor cell-state evolution or causally link stepwise mutation acquisition to transcriptional/epigenetic transitions. Mouse models provide in vivo context but have species-specific developmental programs and limited capacity for human-specific regulatory element interrogation. Patient-derived models preserve heterogeneity but are non-isogenic, preventing controlled dissection of mutation order or allele-specific effects. Prior single-cell studies reveal neuronal- and progenitor-like tumor states and infer trajectories, but they lack matched isogenic perturbations and joint chromatin accessibility measurements to define causal regulators and their binding/activity changes. Methods to date therefore leave unresolved (1) the causal epigenetic mechanisms by which specific driver mutations produce progenitor-like transcriptional programs in human cells, (2) which transcription factors are necessary versus correlative for those transitions in an isogenic background, and (3) how mutation order affects telomerase activation and tumorigenic fitness. Abstract: We describe a reproducible research pipeline to causally map how canonical glioblastoma driver mutations produce tumorigenic cell-state transitions in a human genetic background. The pipeline generates isogenic human embryonic stem cell clones with sequential introduction of TERT promoter C228T, TP53 loss-of-function, and PDGFRA D842V alterations, differentiates them to neural stem cells, and applies integrated single-cell transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility profiling with splicing-based trajectory inference. Epigenetic assays (CUT&RUN/ChIP), telomerase activity measurements, metabolic flux analyses, functional self-renewal and soft-agar assays, orthotopic xenografting, and RNAi/CRISPR perturbations (INSM1, TCF4, SOX4) are used to identify regulatory drivers. The main contribution is a validated pipeline that links stepwise mutation acquisition to emergence of an INSM1-driven intermediate progenitor-like state, defines its chromatin and metabolic dependencies, and tests whether INSM1 inhibition abrogates tumorigenicity. Expected outcomes are (1) allele- and order-specific maps of transcriptional and chromatin changes, (2) identification of TFs whose perturbation alters tumorigenic trajectories, and (3) experimentally supported targets for follow-up therapeutic study. Experiments: 1) Genetic engineering: Generate at least two independent hESC clones per genotype (WT, TERTp C228T heterozygous, TERTp+TP53 R248Q heterozygous, and TERTp+TP53+PDGFRA D842V triple). Use CRISPR/Cas9 HDR for TERTp and TP53 edits and targeted integration or lentiviral expression for PDGFRA D842V. Validate by NGS and Sanger sequencing. 2) Differentiation: Differentiate each clone to adherent neural stem cells (dual SMAD inhibition) and validate PAX6/OCT4 expression. Use two biological replicates per clone. 3) Molecular assays: Measure TERT mRNA by qRT-PCR and telomerase activity by TRAP across genotypes (n=3). Perform CUT&RUN for H3K4me3 and GABP occupancy at the TERT promoter (n=3). 4) In vitro phenotyping: Perform extreme limiting dilution assays (ELDA) for self-renewal (four technical replicates per biological replicate), soft agar colony formation (n=3), and Seahorse assays measuring extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and spare respiratory capacity (n=4). 5) In vivo tumorigenicity: Orthotopically inject 50,000 cells per mouse into athymic nude mice; use n>=10 mice per clone per genotype, monitor by T2 MRI and Kaplan–Meier survival; quantify tumor incidence and volume at fixed timepoints. 6) Single-cell multi-omic profiling: Prepare multiplexed scRNA-seq with hashtag barcodes for pooled WT and mutant NSCs; target >=10,000 cells total, sequencing depth >=20k reads/cell. Perform joint single-nucleus scRNA+ATAC (multiome) for WT and PRO (triple) eNSCs; target >=8k nuclei per condition. Filter thresholds: min genes/cell >=1000, max mitochondrial <=10%. 7) Computational analyses: Normalize with SCTransform, select 2000 HVGs; infer developmental ordering with CytoTRACE; reconstruct RNA velocity using spliced/unspliced counts and dynamical modeling (scVelo/Dynamo); perform Monocle/Slingshot for pseudotime validation; compute motif activity with chromVAR and link peaks with Cicero/LinkPeaks. Define differential peaks (FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>0.5) and DE genes (FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>0.25). 8) Perturbations and ablations: Deliver two independent shRNA/CRISPRi constructs targeting INSM1, TCF4, SOX4 and LacZ control, each barcoded with HTOs; perform pooled scRNA-seq (>=4 conditions) and repeat in vitro assays (ELDA, Seahorse) and in vivo orthotopic assay (n>=10 per condition across two clones). Ablation comparisons: (a) INSM1i vs control in PRO cells; (b) INSM1i vs control in WT cells; (c) TCF4i and SOX4i vs INSM1i; (d) rescue by INSM1 overexpression in INSM1i background. 9) External validation: Test INSM1 perturbation in at least three patient-derived GSC lines representing PRO and non-PRO subtypes; measure ECAR, ELDA, and in vivo tumorigenicity (n>=6 mice per condition for one representative line). 10) Baselines and metrics: Baselines: WT NSCs, single TERTp, and double TERTp+TP53. Evaluation metrics: tumor incidence (%), median survival (days), ELDA-derived stem cell frequency with 95% CI, colony counts (soft agar), ECAR (mpH/min), spare respiratory capacity (% change), telomerase activity units, H3K4me3 and GABP occupancy (% input), counts of DE genes and DARs, motif activity z-scores, change in CytoTRACE score and RNA velocity-predicted fate probabilities. Statistical tests: Kaplan–Meier log-rank for survival; ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc for multi-group comparisons; Wilcoxon rank-sum for two-group single-cell comparisons; adjust p-values by Benjamini–Hochberg; report effect sizes and confidence intervals. 11) Ablation study: Remove TP53 mutation from triple mutant (CRISPR revertant) and repeat assays 3–6 to measure dependence on TP53 for TERT induction and INSM1 program emergence. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: incomplete or mosaic genome editing, unintended off-target edits, and clone-to-clone variability that confound genotype-to-phenotype attribution. Differentiation variability: inconsistent NSC differentiation efficiency or cell-state heterogeneity can obscure mutation-specific effects. Xenograft limitations: variable tumor take rates and species-specific microenvironment interactions reduce translational fidelity and can bias survival metrics. Assay sensitivity: scATAC signal sparsity and low peak recovery per nucleus limit confident motif/activity inference; CUT&RUN/ChIP signal may be low at loci of interest. Computational model limits: RNA velocity and dynamical modeling assume kinetics that may not hold in cancer cells, producing false trajectory inferences; batch effects and sequencing depth differences can bias outcomes. Data biases: reliance on small numbers of clones and cell lines risks overfitting to clonal artifacts and limits generalizability to patient tumors with broader genetic backgrounds. Scalability and cost: multiome and large-scale in vivo cohorts impose high sequencing and animal costs; sample throughput may constrain replication. Biological generalization: findings in engineered heterozygous TERTp/TP53/PDGFRA contexts may not generalize to tumors with alternative driver combinations, differing mutation orders, or additional co-occurring alterations (e.g., ATRX, IDH). Therapeutic translation: INSM1 dependency in vitro or in xenografts may not predict safe or effective targeting in patients due to developmental expression and potential on-target toxicity in normal progenitors.
